newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Kookmin, other Koreans.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Kookmin, other Koreans.

text.p: Kookmin Bank officially launched its HK$1 billion floating rate note issue into Asian debt markets on Monday, one of several Korean issues.
Other Korean deals launched today included a yen bond for Samsung Trading, an FRCD for Saehan Merchant Bank and a samurai for Korea Container Terminal Authority.
Kookmin Bank's first Hong Kong-dollar FRN is a three-year issue launched via Sakura Finance Asia and Merrill Lynch Far East.

It was launched at par and re-offered at 99.85 to float at 40 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Fees are 30 basis points, split evenly between management and underwriting and selling.
The deal was launched off the borrower's Euro medium-term note programme, which is rated A3 by Moody's Investors Service.

With that rating and the size of the HK$1 billion issue, many bankers originally assumed the issue would be eligible for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), or discount window.
Eligibility for LAF makes an issue more attractive to banks because holders of the qualifying debt can engage in repurchase agreements with the monetary authority, increasing liquidity.
But bankers said it later transpired that in order to issue LAF-eligible paper, an issuer must have a branch in Hong Kong, which Kookmin Bank does not.
Still, some bankers said the Kookmin issue is attractive even without LAF status.
"We're definately going to take a piece of it," said one banker, adding that the pricing was right.
In London, Samsung Trading set via Nomura a 12 billion yen straight bond due in October 1999 that pays a coupon of 1.50 percent.
Korea Container Terminal Authority set a 5.0 billion yen Samurai bond due October 2001 that pays a 2.2-percent coupon. Kokusai Securities was lead manager.
Saehan Merchant Bank was in with its US$50 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue launched via IBJ Asia, KDB ASia, LTCB Asia and WestLB Asia Pacific.
The three-year paper pays a coupon of 50 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate and, with fees, an all-in return of 62 basis points.

On the loan side, Indian Oil Corp brought a US$150 million six-month loan through Banque Indosuez and Dresdner Southeast Asia. It pays a margin of 18.5 basis points over LIBOR. Fees are 1-2 basis points.
IOC will use the proceeds to purchase crude oil and petroleum products.
